To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

unexpectedly good accounting and stock price performance have similar short‐run effects, but that the long‐run effect of unexpectedly good accounting performance on CEO pay is significantly negative while the long‐run cumulative effect of unexpectedly good stock price on CEO pay is significant and positive.

unexpectedly good accounting‐based performance is initially associated but ultimately reversed, while unexpectedly good stock price‐based performance is associated with increased compensation for several years.
unexpected accounting performance is associated with a long‐run decline in CEO pay while unexpected stock price performance is positively associated with long‐run CEO pay.

the long‐term effects of firm performance on CEO pay and suggests that stock price performance is a better measure of CEO pay than accounting performance.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CEO pay is more closely related to stock price performance than it is to accounting performance.
CEO pay is more sensitive to stock price performance than to accounting performance.
accounting performance and stock price performance are not necessarily equivalent, and that stock price performance is a better measure of firm performance for the purposes of CEO compensation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CEO's long run financial gain from unexpected performance is significantly higher when the unexpected performance is measured in terms of stock price rather than accounting performance.
accounting‐based performance metrics should be used with caution in dynamic compensation arrangements.
